welcome: Hello Louis! Welcome to Cub Quest. Tonight we can learn about badgers, or foxes, or bats. Which one would you like? Tap a picture.
hello: Hello! This is a badger. Look at the black and white stripes on his face. Badgers live in the woods and the fields, all around Ireland. Can you wave hello to the badger?
stripes: A badger has two black stripes and three white stripes on its face. Every single badger's stripes are a little bit different, just like your fingerprints. Nobody knows for sure why badgers are stripy. Maybe it helps them spot each other in the dark!
night: Badgers sleep all day long, curled up underground. When the sun goes down and the sky goes dark, the badger wakes up, has a big stretch, and pokes his nose outside. Shhh. Can you hear him snuffling?
sett: A badger's home is under the ground. It is called a sett. A really big sett can have more than twenty little rooms, joined up with long, dark, twisty tunnels. That is more rooms than your whole school!
dig: Badgers have long, strong claws on their front paws, like five little spades. They dig, and dig, and dig. A badger can dig a tunnel much faster than you could dig with a big spade. Can you make digging paws with your hands?
worms: Guess what badgers love to eat most of all? Worms! Long, wiggly, slippery worms. A badger can slurp up hundreds of worms in just one night. Slurrrp!
berries: Badgers do not only eat worms. They munch juicy blackberries, and fallen apples, and pears. They crunch up beetles, and slurp up slimy slugs too. Yum! Or maybe... yuck?
cubs: A baby badger is called a cub. Cubs are born deep down inside the sett in the middle of winter, when it is cold and snowy up above. When springtime comes, the cubs come out to play. They love to tumble, and wrestle, and chase each other!
family: Badgers live together in one big family. Sometimes there are more than ten badgers all in the same sett! A daddy badger is called a boar. A mummy badger is called a sow. And a baby badger is a cub.
tidy: Badgers are very tidy. They drag their old grassy bed up out of the sett, and leave it in the sunshine to dry. Then they push fresh grass and leaves back down, for a lovely cosy new bed. Do you make your bed tidy too?
nose: A badger's eyes are quite small, so it cannot see very well at all. But its nose is amazing! A badger can smell a worm hiding under the ground, before it even starts to dig. Sniff, sniff, sniff!
sounds: Badgers make all sorts of funny noises. They purr like a cat. They chatter, and they yelp, and sometimes they growl. A happy little cub purrs when it is snuggled up with its mummy. Can you purr like a badger cub?
qz_badger_daynight: Is a badger awake in the daytime, or at night?
qz_badger_eat: What does a badger like to eat?
qz_badger_math1: A badger found one worm, then found one more worm. How many worms are there now?
qz_badger_math2: Two badger cubs were playing. One more cub came to join them. How many cubs are there now?
qz_badger_math3: There was one juicy berry on the bush. The badger found two more. How many berries are there now?
qz_badger_done: You got all 3 right! Three cheers for a clever cub!
party_badger: Wow! You heard every single badger secret. You are a real badger expert now. Well done, Louis!
party_fox: Brilliant! You know all about foxes now. What a clever fox you are. Well done, Louis!
party_bat: Amazing! You have learned every single bat secret. You are a bat expert now. Well done, Louis!
fox_hello: Hello! This is a fox. Look at her beautiful orange fur, her white tummy, and her big bushy tail. Foxes live all over Ireland. In the fields, in the woods, and even in towns and cities.
madra: In Irish, a fox is called a madra rua. That means red dog! A fox really is a kind of wild dog. But she does lots of things that cats do, too.
brush: A fox's big fluffy tail has a special name. It is called a brush, and it has a little white tip on the end. When a fox curls up to go to sleep, she wraps her brush right over her nose, like a cosy scarf.
earth: A fox's home is a burrow under the ground. It is called an earth. Sometimes a fox digs her own earth, and sometimes she moves into an old badger sett. In a town, a fox might make her earth underneath a garden shed!
ears: A fox has the most amazing ears. She can turn each ear round on its own, to listen in different directions. She can hear a tiny mouse rustling about in the long grass, far, far away.
pounce: When a fox hears a mouse hiding in the grass, she does something very funny. First she stands as still as a statue. Then she jumps high up into the air, and dives straight down, nose first! Can you do a fox pounce?
eyes: Look closely at a fox's eyes. They have a thin black line down the middle, just like a cat's eyes. A fox can see brilliantly in the dark. That is why she loves to come out at night time.
whiskers: Foxes have whiskers on their face, just like a cat does. But guess what? They have whiskers on their legs as well! The whiskers help the fox feel her way through dark and narrow places.
foxeats: Foxes eat almost anything they can find. Mice and rabbits, beetles and wriggly worms, and lots and lots of juicy blackberries. Town foxes love to nibble the food that people drop.
bury: When a fox finds more food than she can eat, she does not leave it behind. She digs a little hole, pops the food inside, and pushes the soil back over it with her nose. Then she comes back for it later. A secret snack box!
foxcubs: Baby foxes are called cubs. They are born in the springtime, deep down inside the earth. When they are tiny they are dark and fluffy, and their eyes are shut tight. After a few weeks their fur turns red, and out they come to play.
foxnoises: Foxes are very noisy at night. A daddy fox is called a dog fox, and he barks. It sounds like wow, wow, wow. A mummy fox is called a vixen, and she makes a loud screechy noise that sounds a little bit spooky!
bat_hello: Hello! This is a bat. Bats come out when the sky goes dark, and they whizz and swoop about, catching little insects. There are nine different kinds of bat living in Ireland.
bat_fly: Here is something very special about bats. Bats are the only furry animal in the whole wide world that can really and truly fly. Not glide, not jump. Fly! Just like a bird, but with fur.
bat_hands: A bat's wing is really its hand. Imagine if your fingers grew, and grew, and grew, until they were nearly as long as your whole body. Then imagine soft stretchy skin joining them all together. That is a bat's wing!
bat_ears: When a bat flies in the dark, it shouts out loud. Then it listens for the echo bouncing back. The echo tells the bat exactly where everything is. It is called echolocation. The shouts are far too squeaky for you and me to hear.
bat_see: Some people say, as blind as a bat. But that is not true at all! Every single bat in the world can see perfectly well. It is just that in the dark, a bat's ears are even more useful than its eyes.
bat_tiny: The smallest Irish bat is called a pipistrelle. It weighs about the same as one little coin. With its wings folded up, it could curl up and fit inside a matchbox. Its body is only about as big as your thumb!
bat_eat: Bats are very hungry little creatures. One tiny pipistrelle can gobble up about three thousand midges in a single night. That is why you get fewer itchy bites in the garden when the bats are out. Thank you, bats!
bat_upside: One kind of Irish bat likes to sleep hanging upside down, holding on with its toes. Its toes grip tight all by themselves, even when it is fast asleep. And here is a funny thing. A bat's knees bend the opposite way to yours!
bat_bigears: The brown long eared bat has ears almost as long as its whole body. It is so quiet and so sneaky that it listens for little insects wriggling about on the leaves. When it goes to sleep, it curls its ears up, like two little ram's horns.
bat_roost: A bat's home is called a roost. Bats do not build a nest. Instead they squeeze into cosy little cracks and gaps. Under the roof tiles of a house, inside a hole in an old tree, and even in the stones of a bridge.
bat_winter: In the wintertime all the insects disappear, so the bats go to sleep for months and months. When a bat is flying, its heart beats more than a thousand times every minute. But when it is fast asleep in winter, it beats only four times a minute!
bat_pups: A baby bat is called a pup. A mummy bat usually has just one pup each year, in the summertime. She feeds her pup with milk, and cuddles it close. After about three weeks, the little pup can fly all by itself.
party_hedgehog: Wonderful! You have learned every single hedgehog secret. Well done, Louis!
party_owl: Fantastic! You know all about barn owls now. What a wise owl you are. Well done, Louis!
party_otter: Splendid! You have found every single otter secret. Well done, Louis!
hh_hello: Hello! This is a hedgehog. He is round and prickly, and he comes out at night to hunt for his dinner. You might find one snuffling about in a garden, or under a hedge.
hh_spines: A hedgehog has thousands and thousands of spines on his back. More than five thousand! And here is the surprise. The spines are not thorns at all. They are just very hard hairs, made of exactly the same stuff as your fingernails.
hh_ball: When a hedgehog gets a fright, he rolls himself up into a tight little ball. He has a special muscle across his back, like a cape, that pulls his prickly skin all the way round him. Now he is a spiky ball, and nothing can nibble him.
hh_legs: Hedgehogs look very short and round. But underneath all those spines they have surprisingly long legs! A hedgehog can trot along quite fast, and he might walk two whole kilometres in just one night, looking for food.
hh_eats: What does a hedgehog like to eat? Creepy crawlies! Beetles and earwigs, wriggly worms and slugs, caterpillars and millipedes. He snuffles along the ground with his nose down, sniffing them out.
hh_winter: When winter comes, a hedgehog goes to sleep for months and months. His heart slows right down, from nearly two hundred beats a minute to only twenty. He gets cold and still, and he breathes just once every few minutes. He looks almost like he is not there at all.
hh_nest: Before his big sleep, a hedgehog builds himself a cosy winter nest out of dry leaves. He pushes and pushes until the walls are as thick as your hand. Then he curls up in the middle, all snug, and sleeps until springtime.
hh_hoglets: A baby hedgehog is called a hoglet. When a hoglet is born he cannot see at all, and he has no spikes, so he does not hurt his mummy. Then, only a few hours later, tiny white spines start to push their way out through his skin.
hh_anoint: Hedgehogs do the strangest thing of any animal in Ireland. When a hedgehog smells something new, he chews and chews until his mouth is full of froth. Then he flicks the froth all over his own spines with his tongue! Nobody in the whole world knows why he does it.
hh_noise: Hedgehogs are surprisingly noisy. They snuffle and they huff and they snort, especially when two of them meet. And a tiny hoglet makes a little whistling squeak when he is calling for his mummy.
hh_myth: Some picture books show a hedgehog with an apple stuck on his spines, carrying it home for his tea. But that is just a story! Real hedgehogs never do that. They do not carry their food at all, and they do not even like apples very much.
hh_help: Would you like to help a hedgehog? Leave out a little bowl of water, and some meaty cat food. But never, ever give a hedgehog milk. Milk gives hedgehogs a very poorly tummy. And leave a small gap under the garden fence, so he can trundle through.
bo_hello: Hello! This is a barn owl. Look at her beautiful white heart shaped face and her golden wings. Barn owls live in Ireland, and they love to make their home in old ruined castles.
bo_silent: A barn owl flies more quietly than any other bird. If you were standing right underneath, you would not hear a thing. The front edge of her wing has a row of tiny soft combs on it, and they hush the sound of the air rushing past.
bo_why: Why does an owl need to fly so quietly? Not just so the mice cannot hear her coming. It is so that she can hear them! If her wings made a swooshing noise, it would cover up the tiny rustling sounds she is listening for.
bo_face: A barn owl's face is shaped like a big white heart. That shape is not just for looking pretty. It works like a dish, catching all the little sounds from the field below and funnelling them straight into her ears.
bo_ears: Here is a funny thing about a barn owl. Her two ears are not the same. One ear is a bit higher up than the other one! That means a sound reaches one ear a tiny bit before the other, and her clever brain works out exactly where the mouse is.
bo_dark: A barn owl can catch a mouse in the pitch dark. Not dim light. Completely, totally dark, with nothing to see at all. She finds it just by listening. Her hearing is some of the best hearing of any animal in the whole world.
bo_pellets: A barn owl swallows a mouse whole, in one gulp! But she cannot eat the bones and the fur. So a little while later she coughs them back up, all squished into a neat furry parcel. It is called a pellet. If you pull one apart, you can find all the little bones inside.
bo_food: A hungry barn owl eats about four little mice and voles every single night. Four every night, all year long, adds up to more than a thousand. That is a lot of mice!
bo_screech: Do you know what noise a barn owl makes? She does not go too whit, too woo. That is a different owl, called a tawny owl. A barn owl screeches! It is a long, loud, screechy shriek in the dark.
bo_eggs: A barn owl does not build a nest. Not one single twig! She lays her eggs straight down on the floor of an old barn or a castle. She lays about five eggs, but not all on the same day. She lays one, then waits two or three days, then lays another.
bo_owlets: Baby owls are called owlets, and they hatch out with no feathers at all. Because the eggs were laid on different days, the biggest owlet can be three whole weeks older than the smallest one. And here is the loveliest thing. Owlets have been seen giving their food to their little brothers and sisters.
bo_rain: You might think a bird that lives outside would have waterproof feathers. But a barn owl's feathers are not waterproof at all! When it rains hard, she gets soaked right through, so she has to stay tucked up somewhere dry until it stops.
ot_hello: Hello! This is an otter. She lives beside rivers and lakes, and she is a brilliant swimmer. Ireland is one of the very best places in the whole of Europe to be an otter.
ot_fur: An otter swims in cold water all day, but her skin never gets wet. She wears two coats! The outside coat keeps the water off, and the fluffy coat underneath is so thick that it traps a layer of warm air right next to her skin.
ot_shut: When an otter dives under the water, she can shut her ears and shut her nose, all by herself. No water can get in. Can you hold your nose and shut your eyes? An otter does not even need her hands.
ot_whisk: River water is often muddy and dark, so an otter cannot see very much down there. But she has long, wobbly whiskers on her face. When a fish swishes past, the whiskers feel the water wobble, and she knows exactly where it went.
ot_eyes: An otter's eyes are right on top of her head. That is very handy. She can float with her whole body hidden under the water, with just her eyes peeping out, having a good look around.
ot_dive: An otter does not stay under the water for very long. Most of her dives are only about thirty seconds. Down she goes, a quick wriggly hunt, and up she pops again. Can you count to thirty?
ot_fish: Otters love to eat fish, more than anything else. Little tiny sticklebacks, big slippery eels, and even salmon. She holds the fish in her front paws and crunches it up, head first.
ot_holt: An otter's home is called a holt. It is a snug den hidden under a pile of rocks, or in among the twisty roots of a big old tree by the water. A holt has several different doors, and one of them is always up high, so it never floods.
ot_cubs: A baby otter is called a cub. Otters usually have two or three cubs, and when they are born they are tiny, only about as big as your hand. They stay hidden away safe inside the holt for the first ten weeks.
ot_swim: Here is something surprising about otters. Baby otters cannot swim! Not for a long time. A little cub does not go into the water until he is a few months old. He stays with his mummy for nearly a whole year before he goes off on his own.
ot_spraint: Otters leave messages for each other. An otter does a poo on a big rock beside the river, and it tells the other otters that she has been there. It is called spraint. It is full of shiny fish bones, and funnily enough, people say it smells rather nice.
ot_prints: Would you like to find out if an otter has been by the river? Look for footprints in the mud. A dog print or a fox print has four toes. But an otter print has five! Five little toes, and sometimes some webbing in between them.
party_marten: Amazing! You have found every single pine marten secret. They are very hard to find. Well done, Louis!
pm_hello: Hello! This is a pine marten. She is about as big as a cat, with soft chestnut brown fur, big round ears, and a long bushy tail. She lives up in the woods, and she is very, very good at climbing.
pm_cat: In Irish, a pine marten is called a cat crainn. That means tree cat! But she is not really a cat at all. She is a cousin of the badger, and the otter, and the stoat.
pm_bib: Every pine marten has a splodge of creamy orange fur on her chest. It is called a bib. And here is the clever part. Every single marten's bib is a different shape, just like fingerprints. That is how people tell them apart.
pm_climb: A pine marten is a brilliant climber. Her ankles can turn the whole way round, so she can run back down a tree just as fast as she ran up it! She can leap a long way too, and if she does fall, she twists in the air and lands on her feet.
pm_squeeze: A pine marten can squeeze through a hole no wider than a golf ball. If her head fits through, the rest of her can wriggle after it. That is how she gets into all sorts of hidey holes.
pm_den: A pine marten sleeps in a den, high up inside a hole in an old tree. Sometimes she borrows a squirrel's nest instead, or squeezes into a crack in the rocks. Ireland does not have many really old trees any more, so kind people build her wooden boxes to sleep in.
pm_berries: A pine marten has a very sweet tooth. In the summertime, nearly a third of everything she eats is berries! And if you leave a jam sandwich or some peanuts out in the garden, a pine marten might just come and take them.
pm_poo: Here is a funny thing. A pine marten's poo smells lovely. Really! People say it smells sweet, a bit like flowers. She leaves it right in the middle of the path, to tell the other martens that this is her wood. And after she has eaten lots of berries, it turns blue!
pm_squirrels: Something wonderful happened when the pine martens came back. Red squirrels came back too! Red squirrels have lived with pine martens for thousands and thousands of years, so they know exactly how to keep out of the way. But grey squirrels came here from far away, and they never learned how.
pm_kits: Baby pine martens are called kits. There are usually two or three of them, born in the springtime, high up in the tree. A newborn kit is tiny, about as heavy as a little battery, and its eyes are shut tight. It stays in the den for six or seven weeks before it peeps out.
pm_rare: The pine marten is the rarest animal in Ireland. Long ago there were hardly any left at all. But people looked after them, and slowly, slowly, they came back. Now there are pine martens in every single county. You would be very lucky indeed to see one.
pm_noise: Pine martens are usually very quiet. But in the summertime they make a loud, shrill yowling noise, a bit like a cross cat on a rooftop. And when the kits are big enough to play, they can be noisy all night long!
party_stoat: Brilliant! You have learned every single stoat secret. Well done, Louis!
party_frog: Wonderful! You know all about frogs now. Hop hop hooray! Well done, Louis!
party_moth: Marvellous! You have found every single moth secret. Well done, Louis!
st_hello: Hello! This is a stoat. She is long and thin and very, very quick, with a chestnut brown back and a creamy white tummy. Look at the tip of her tail. It is jet black.
st_easog: In Irish, a stoat is called an easóg. Stoats live all over Ireland, in the hedges and the ditches and the old stone walls. But they move so fast that you hardly ever see one.
st_weasel: Lots of people in Ireland call this little animal a weasel. But here is the funny thing. There are no weasels in Ireland at all! Not a single one. Every time somebody spots a weasel here, it is really a stoat.
st_tail: Why does a stoat have a black tip on her tail? Clever scientists think it is a trick. When a big hungry bird swoops down, it grabs at the black spot, because it is easy to see. So the bird gets a mouthful of tail, and the stoat runs away safely.
st_thin: A stoat is shaped like a furry little sausage. She is so long and so thin that she can follow a mouse right down into its tunnel, and pop out the other end. She can climb trees, and swim, and squeeze through the tiniest gaps in a stone wall.
st_big: A stoat is only about as long as a ruler. But she is very brave. A stoat can catch a rabbit that is five times bigger than she is, and carry it all the way home!
st_white: In cold snowy countries, stoats turn snowy white in the winter, so nobody can see them. But Irish stoats stay brown all year round. That is because Ireland hardly ever gets deep snow. A white stoat here would stick out like a sore thumb!
st_den: A stoat does not dig her own burrow. She moves into a hole that used to belong to somebody else, and she makes it cosy with soft fur and feathers. She is a bit of a cheeky house guest.
st_awake: Some animals sleep all day. Some sleep all winter. A stoat does neither! A stoat is busy in the daytime and busy at night time, every single day of the year. She is always, always hunting.
st_kits: Baby stoats are called kits. A mummy stoat might have ten kits all at once, tucked up together in her den. They are born in the springtime, and when they are little they cannot see or hear a thing.
st_wait: Stoats do something very strange indeed. A mummy stoat gets her babies started in the summertime. But then they stop, and they wait, and they wait, all the way through autumn and winter. They do not start growing again until the spring!
st_old: Stoats have lived in Ireland for a very, very long time. Longer than badgers. Longer than foxes. People have found stoat bones here that are more than thirty thousand years old. Stoats were running about in Ireland before the ice age, during the ice age, and after it too.
fr_hello: Hello! This is a frog. Frogs live in ponds and ditches, and in any damp shady spot they can find. There is only one kind of frog in the whole of Ireland, and this is it.
fr_loscan: In Irish, a frog is called a loscán. Frogs have lived here for thousands and thousands of years, ever since the ice melted away. There are more frogs in Ireland than almost any other animal.
fr_spawn: In February, when it is still cold, the frogs all wake up and hop back to their pond. Then the mummy frog lays her eggs in the water. Not two or three eggs. Not ten. She lays about two thousand! They float in a big wobbly clump of jelly, called frogspawn.
fr_tadpole: After two or three weeks, something tiny wriggles out of each little egg. A tadpole! A baby tadpole has no legs at all. It has a long wiggly tail for swimming, and fluffy little gills so it can breathe under the water, just like a fish.
fr_legs: Now watch what happens. After about five weeks, two little back legs pop out. Then, a few weeks later, two front legs appear as well. The tadpole is growing lungs inside, so it starts swimming up to gulp air at the top of the pond.
fr_froglet: And then the strangest thing of all. The tadpole's tail gets shorter, and shorter, and shorter, until it disappears completely! After about fourteen weeks there is no tadpole left. There is a tiny little frog, hopping out of the pond.
fr_skin: A frog can breathe through its skin! Its skin is so thin that air can pass straight through it, even underwater. But that only works if the frog stays nice and damp. That is why you find frogs in wet, shady, squelchy places.
fr_winter: Where does a frog go in the winter? Some of them wriggle down into the soft muddy silt at the very bottom of the pond, and they stay there all winter long, hardly moving. They do not need to come up for air, because they are breathing through their skin.
fr_colour: Frogs come in all sorts of colours. Green, brown, yellow, and sometimes even reddish. And a frog can change its own colour! If it sits somewhere dark, it slowly goes darker to match. It takes about two hours.
fr_tongue: A frog's tongue is not stuck on at the back like yours. It is joined on at the front! So the frog can flip it out forwards, very fast, and catch a fly on the sticky end. Then the whole thing folds back in, with dinner attached.
fr_croak: In the springtime the boy frogs all sit in the pond and croak together. Croak, croak, croak! It is a proper froggy choir. And if something grabs hold of a frog, it can let out a loud, high squeaky scream to give the fright of its life.
fr_lots: Would you like to know how many frogs there are in Ireland? Nobody can count them all, but clever people think there are more than a hundred million. So next time you are near a pond, have a good look. There might be one hiding right beside you.
mo_hello: Hello! This is a moth. Moths come out when it goes dark, and they flutter about in the night. There are about one thousand five hundred different kinds of moth in Ireland. And only thirty five kinds of butterfly!
mo_vs: How can you tell a moth from a butterfly? Look at the little feelers on its head. A butterfly's feelers have a tiny bobble on the end, like a lollipop. A moth's are feathery, or they come to a fine point. And when a moth has a rest, it lays its wings out flat.
mo_day: Here is something that surprises people. Not all moths fly at night! Lots and lots of moths come out in the sunshine, just like butterflies do. So if you see something fluttering about in the daytime, do not be too sure it is a butterfly.
mo_tongue: A moth does not have a mouth for chewing. It has a long, thin tongue, curled up underneath its head like a party blower. When it finds a flower, it unrolls its tongue and sucks up the sweet nectar, like drinking through a straw.
mo_life: A moth does not start off as a moth. First it is a tiny egg. Then a hungry caterpillar comes out and eats, and eats, and eats. Then it wraps itself up and goes very still. And when it comes out again, it is a moth with wings!
mo_cocoon: When a caterpillar is ready to change, it spins itself a little silk sleeping bag. It is called a cocoon. One moth, called the puss moth, mixes its silk with chewed up bark and makes a cocoon so hard that you could not squash it with your fingers.
mo_light: Why do moths go round and round a lamp at night? Scientists have only just worked this out. A moth always keeps its back pointed towards the brightest light, because usually the brightest thing is the sky. But when the brightest thing is a lamp, the poor moth ends up flying in circles all around it.
mo_bats: Moths have to watch out for hungry bats. So lots of moths have little ears that can hear a bat shouting! When they hear it coming, they tumble out of the way. And some clever moths click back at the bat, to muddle it up completely.
mo_pollen: While you are fast asleep, the moths are busy helping the flowers. When a moth drinks nectar, sticky yellow pollen sticks to its furry body, and it carries the pollen to the next flower. Moths do this even faster than bees do.
mo_elephant: One of the prettiest moths in Ireland is the elephant hawk moth. It is bright pink and green, like a birthday cake. And its caterpillar has a very good trick. When something frightens it, it puffs itself up so it looks just like a snake, with big scary eyes!
mo_emperor: The emperor moth has four big spots on its wings that look exactly like eyes, to give the birds a fright. And here is the strangest thing about it. A grown up emperor moth does not eat anything at all. It has no mouth to eat with!
mo_clothes: People say that moths eat your jumpers. But out of all those hundreds and hundreds of moths, only two little kinds ever do that. And it is not the moths, it is their caterpillars. They only nibble woolly things. So nearly every moth is completely innocent!
party_seal: Wonderful! You have learned every single seal secret. Well done, Louis!
party_puffin: Brilliant! You know all about puffins now. Well done, Louis!
party_dolphin: Amazing! You have found every single dolphin secret. Well done, Louis!
party_shark: Fantastic! You know all about the biggest fish in Ireland. Well done, Louis!
sl_hello: Hello! This is a grey seal. In Irish he is called a rón mór, which means big seal. There are about fifteen thousand grey seals splashing about around Ireland, so he has plenty of friends.
sl_nose: There are two kinds of seal in Ireland, and here is how to tell them apart. A grey seal has a long straight nose, a bit like a big friendly dog. The other one, the harbour seal, has a squashed in face more like a cat. Look at the nose!
sl_pup: Baby seals are called pups. They are born on quiet stony beaches in the autumn, and they come out wearing a coat of fluffy white fur. It keeps them beautifully warm. But it is not waterproof, so a little pup cannot go swimming yet.
sl_milk: A mummy seal's milk is the creamiest milk in the world. More than half of it is pure fat! A seal pup drinks and drinks and puts on about two kilograms every single day. In three weeks he is three times as big as when he was born.
sl_dive: A grey seal can hold his breath for a very long time. Not one minute. Not five minutes. A grey seal can stay under the water for half an hour! And he can dive down deeper than a tall church steeple.
sl_whiskers: A seal's whiskers are magic. When a fish swims past, it leaves a little wobbly trail in the water behind it, like the wobble behind a boat. A seal's whiskers can feel that wobble, and follow it, even when the fish is long gone and the water is dark and muddy.
sl_sleep: Where does a seal sleep? Sometimes on a rock. But sometimes he sleeps right in the sea, bobbing upright with just his nose sticking out, like a bottle floating. He sleeps with half of his brain at a time, so the other half can remember to breathe.
sl_sing: Seals are very noisy. They moan and they howl and they make long wobbly singing sounds that float across the water. Some people think that is where the old Irish stories about seal people came from. Sailors heard the singing, and wondered what it was.
sl_eat: Seals eat fish. Lots and lots of fish. A great big grey seal might eat fifteen kilograms in one day. That is heavier than a big bag of potatoes. He likes sand eels and cod, and sometimes a crab or a squid for a treat.
sl_where: Would you like to see a seal? The best places in Ireland are the quiet islands. The Inishkea Islands in Mayo have more seals than anywhere else. There are lots on the Blasket Islands in Kerry, and the Saltee Islands in Wexford too.
sl_found: If you ever find a baby seal on a beach, here is what to do. Stay far, far away. Do not touch him. Do not put him back in the sea, because he is on the sand for a good reason. His mummy is probably watching from the water. Tell a grown up, and they can ring the seal rescue people.
sl_big: Grey seals are enormous. A big daddy seal can weigh three hundred kilograms. That is heavier than four grown ups all squashed together! Under his skin he has a thick layer of blubber to keep him warm, as thick as your finger is long.
pf_hello: Hello! This is a puffin. In Irish he is called a puifín. He has a black coat, a white tummy, bright orange feet, and the most colourful beak of any bird in Ireland. Puffins live on rocky islands right out in the sea.
pf_beak: A puffin's beak is stripy orange and yellow and blue, like a little painted boat. But only in the summertime! When winter comes, the bright colours peel away and fall off, and the beak turns a plain dull grey. Then next spring, the colours come back again.
pf_fish: A puffin can carry a lot of fish in his beak at once. How many do you think? Ten? Twenty? The record is eighty three little fish, all lined up sideways! His tongue holds them tight against tiny spikes on the roof of his mouth, so he can open his beak and catch more without dropping any.
pf_fly: Puffins are round and heavy with very small wings, so flying is hard work. A puffin has to flap four hundred times every minute just to stay up in the air! But once he gets going, he can whizz along faster than a car on the motorway.
pf_swim: A puffin does not paddle with his feet when he dives. He flaps his wings and flies along underwater! He can swim down deeper than a house is tall, chasing little fish, and stay under for more than a minute before popping back up.
pf_burrow: A puffin does not build a nest in a tree. He nests in a burrow, in a hole in the grassy top of a cliff. And sometimes, if he finds a nice rabbit hole, he simply moves in and shoos the rabbit out. Cheeky!
pf_egg: A mummy puffin lays just one egg each year. Only one! She tucks it away at the very back of the burrow where it is dark and safe, and she and the daddy puffin take turns keeping it warm until it hatches.
pf_puffling: A baby puffin has the best name of any baby animal. It is called a puffling! The puffling stays hidden down in the burrow, and its mummy and daddy bring it fish for about six weeks, until it is big enough to go out to the sea.
pf_sea: Puffins only come to Ireland for the summer. For the rest of the year, all eight months of it, they live right out in the middle of the ocean, bobbing about on the waves, miles and miles from any land at all. They even sleep out there.
pf_pair: Puffins keep the same friend for a very long time. A puffin pair can stay together for more than twenty years, and they come back to the very same burrow every summer. When they meet again, they tap their beaks together to say hello.
pf_monk: The puffin's proper scientific name means little brother. People thought that his black and white feathers looked like the robes of a monk. And there is an old Irish story that puffins carried the souls of the monks who once lived out on Skellig Michael.
pf_trouble: Puffins need our help. There are far fewer puffins in Ireland than there used to be, and every year there are fewer still. The seas are changing and there are not as many little fish for them to catch. So if you ever see one, look after him.
dl_hello: Hello! This is a bottlenose dolphin. Dolphins are not fish at all. They are warm and furry when they are born, they breathe air just like you, and their mummies feed them milk. A dolphin is a bit like a very clever swimming puppy.
dl_shannon: There is a family of dolphins that lives in the river Shannon all year round. Just there, and nowhere else. There are more than a hundred of them, and they are a little bit different from every other dolphin in the world. They are Ireland's own dolphins.
dl_click: How does a dolphin find a fish in the dark deep water? She shouts! She makes little clicking noises that whizz through the water, bounce off the fish, and come whizzing back to her. She hears the echo through her jawbone. She is seeing with sound.
dl_sleep: A dolphin can never fall properly asleep, because she has to remember to come up and breathe. So she sleeps with only half of her brain at a time, and she closes only one eye! Later on, she swaps over and sleeps with the other half.
dl_breathe: A dolphin breathes through a hole on the top of her head, called a blowhole. When she comes up, it opens with a big puff, and then it snaps shut before she goes back under. You and I breathe without thinking. A dolphin has to think about every single breath.
dl_name: Here is the most amazing thing about dolphins. Every dolphin makes up her very own special whistle when she is little, and she keeps it forever. All the other dolphins learn it. When they want to call her, they whistle her whistle. Dolphins have names!
dl_fast: A dolphin usually swims along quite slowly. But if she is in a hurry, she can zoom through the water as fast as a car! She loves to leap right up out of the sea, and she will race along in front of a boat, riding the wave the boat pushes.
dl_calf: A baby dolphin is called a calf. She swims beside her mummy from the very first day, drinking her milk under the water. Her mummy teaches her how to catch fish, and that takes years and years of practice.
dl_porpoise: Sometimes people see a porpoise and think it is a dolphin. Here is how to tell. A dolphin has a little pointy beak like a bottle, and she jumps and shows off. A porpoise has a round face with no beak at all, and she is shy, and pops up quietly for just a moment.
dl_sanctuary: A very long time before you were born, Ireland did something wonderful. In nineteen ninety one, Ireland said that all the seas around the whole country would be a safe place where nobody is ever allowed to hurt a whale or a dolphin. Ireland was the very first country in Europe to do it.
dl_fungie: In Dingle there once lived a dolphin called Fungie. He did not live with the other dolphins. He lived all by himself in the harbour for many, many years, and he loved to swim beside the boats and say hello to people. Then one day, when he was very old, he swam away, and nobody knows where he went.
dl_many: Dolphins are not the only ones out there. More than twenty different kinds of whales and dolphins and porpoises have been spotted swimming in the sea around Ireland. Some of them are absolutely enormous. You never know what you might see.
bs_hello: Hello! This is a basking shark. He is the biggest fish in Ireland, and the second biggest fish in the whole wide world. He can grow as long as a bus. In Irish he has a lovely name. He is called the liamhán gréine.
bs_harmless: Now, he is a shark, and he is enormous. But do not be frightened of him! A basking shark would never ever hurt you. He does not eat fish, or seals, or people. He only eats plankton, which is teeny tiny wiggly creatures, far too small for you to see.
bs_mouth: A basking shark has the most enormous mouth. It is wider than your arms can stretch! He swims along very slowly with his mouth wide open, letting the sea pour in one end and out through his gills at the other, and keeping all the little bits to eat.
bs_filter: How much water goes through that big mouth? In just one hour, a basking shark strains more than a million litres of sea water. That is enough to fill half of a great big swimming pool. Every hour! All day long.
bs_teeth: Here is a funny thing about the basking shark. He still has teeth. About one thousand five hundred of them! But each tooth is only as big as a grain of rice, and he never uses them for anything at all. He just has them.
bs_name: People named him the basking shark because he floats near the top of the sea and looks like he is lying in the sunshine, having a lovely rest. But he is not resting at all. That is where all the little plankton float, so really, he is just having his dinner.
bs_ireland: Ireland is one of the best places in the whole world to see a basking shark. There are lots of them off the coast of Donegal, and Kerry, and Cork, especially in the springtime. Out of all the basking sharks anywhere, a great many of them come to visit us.
bs_many: Basking sharks like company. Usually you might see one, or maybe two. But sometimes, when there is lots and lots of plankton, they all come together. Once, off the coast of Ireland, somebody counted seventy five basking sharks all swimming in the very same place.
bs_deep: In the wintertime the basking sharks disappear. For years and years nobody knew where they went. Now we know. They swim down, and down, and down, deeper than a mountain is tall, and they travel enormous distances across the ocean, following their dinner.
bs_jump: A basking shark weighs as much as an elephant. But sometimes, he jumps! He swims up fast from far below and launches himself right out of the water, all of him, and lands again with the most tremendous splash. Nobody is quite sure why he does it.
bs_warm: Here is something very new. Almost every fish in the sea is cold inside, as cold as the water around it. But in Ireland, only a few years ago, some scientists in Dublin discovered that the basking shark is different. He keeps himself warm inside. Nobody had any idea!
bs_safe: For a long time people hunted basking sharks in Ireland, and there got to be very few of them left. But now they are looked after. A few years ago Ireland made a special new rule, and the basking shark became the very first fish in the whole country to be properly protected.
